name: The Plane Tree of the Harmonie
age_estimate: roughly 205 to 215 years, from the register's planting band of 1810 to 1820

location.address: Beside the main entrance of Theater De Harmonie, Ruiterskwartier, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1682933, London Plane, planted band 1810-1820)
https://periodieken.historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/issue/TKK/1991-06-01/edition/null/page/3 ('t Kleine Krantsje, 1 June 1991, readers' letters page)
access: Free. Stands on the public square beside the theatre's main entrance.
transport: Central Leeuwarden, short walk from Leeuwarden Centraal station.
verify_notes: Register nr 1682933, planted band 1810-1820, next to the main entrance of Theater/Stadsschouwburg De Harmonie. A 1991 letters-page item in 't Kleine Krantsje (a Leeuwarden local-history periodical, HCL's own digitised archive) independently names this exact tree: it calls it 'de meer dan honderd jaar oude plataan bij de Harmonie' (the plane tree by the Harmonie, more than a hundred years old) and describes it as the subject of public concern in 1991 over renovation works that threatened to remove it, with the writer hoping the council would yield to public pressure, drawing a parallel to an old beech at the Princessehof saved by protest decades earlier (that beech, register nr 1682922, was ultimately felled in 2015 per the register, so the parallel held only for a while). The register's 2024 edition carries no removal note for this plane, unlike the Princessehof beeches which explicitly do, so treat it as standing. No girth or exact height found this pass.
story:
In 1991 a reader wrote in to a Leeuwarden local-history paper to defend this tree. Renovation work at De Harmonie was expected to take out the plane beside the main entrance, and the letter asked the council to give way to public pressure, as it had done decades earlier over an old beech at the Princessehof. The plane is still standing. The beech is not. The register records it as felled in 2015, so the precedent held for a while and then it did not.

The letter called it the plane by the Harmonie, more than a hundred years old, which undersold it considerably. The national register of monumental trees puts its planting between 1810 and 1820, closer to two centuries than to one. That band brackets the end of French rule in the Netherlands, which fell away in 1813, so the tree was a sapling in a city that had just changed countries.

Everything around it has changed use at least once since. The tree has not moved, and it still holds the corner of the square where people queue to get into a show. Nobody has recorded a girth or a height for it, which is a gap a tape measure and one message would close.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flaking patchwork bark that only a plane has, cream over olive where the old plates come away. It stands on the public square at the Ruiterskwartier, right beside the main entrance of Theater De Harmonie.

name: The Horse Chestnut of Blokhuispoort
age_estimate: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: Keizersgracht / Oosterkade, beside the former Huis van Bewaring (Blokhuispoort)

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1682930, planted band 1880-1890)
access: Free. Stands on the public quay/street beside the former Huis van Bewaring at Blokhuispoort, on the Keizersgracht/Oosterkade side of the complex (a different corner from the Crimean linden already on this site, lee_022, which stands at the Blokhuisplein entrance about 550m away).
transport: About 700 m southeast of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
verify_notes: Register nr 1682930. The Blokhuispoort complex began as a 15th-century citadel (Blokhuis), gained a cell wing in 1892-1894 when this chestnut was likely planted, and is now a public library, cultural venue and shops. The register notes sulphur-tuft fungus (zwavelkopjeszwam, a white-rot fungus) found at the base at a 2017-ish inspection but rates the tree's condition as good and says it can safely remain. It also notes the growing site has increasingly been used as a car park, with only a small green strip on the canal side. No second independent source found this pass; single-sourced on the register. Only about 550m from lee_022 (Crimean Linden, Blokhuisplein), a different tree at a different corner of the same historic complex.
story:
This chestnut spent most of its life outside a prison and now stands outside a library.

The Blokhuispoort started as a fifteenth-century citadel, the blokhuis the name comes from, and became the Huis van Bewaring, the city house of detention. Its cell wing went up between 1892 and 1894. The register dates the chestnut to somewhere between 1880 and 1890, so it was in the ground before the masons arrived, and it kept its corner while the cells filled and emptied for the better part of a century. The doors are open now. The complex holds the public library, workspaces and shops, and the walls are one of the few places in Leeuwarden where you can read a book where people once were not allowed to leave.

Inspectors found sulphur tuft at the foot of the trunk, a white-rot fungus, at a check around 2017. They rated the tree good anyway and concluded it can safely stay. The ground has been less generous than the inspectors: the register notes that the growing space has increasingly gone over to parked cars, leaving a thin green strip on the canal side.

About a hundred and forty years of that, and it still drops conkers every autumn. Only the register has written this one up, so if you know more of its story, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the horse chestnut hand of five to seven leaflets spreading from one stalk, and by the cars parked to its foot. It stands on the Keizersgracht quay side of the Blokhuispoort, not at the Blokhuisplein entrance.

best_time.label: late September into October, when the conkers come down on the quay

name: The Horse Chestnut of Spanjaardslaan
age_estimate: roughly 116 to 126 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1682935, planted band 1900-1910)
https://regioonline.nl/regio-leeuwarden/leeuwarden-spanjaardslaan-bomen/ (RondOm/RegioOnline, 25 April 2025, on chestnut disease along this street)
access: Free. Stands on the public Spanjaardslaan street, a residential avenue lined with chestnuts.
transport: About 1.2 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
verify_notes: Register nr 1682935 gives no place detail beyond the street name and no condition note ('onbekend'). A 25 April 2025 local news item confirms a genuine risk context for this exact street: a large number of the white and red horse chestnuts on Spanjaardslaan are in poor condition from bleeding canker, one tree at house number 134 was felled the same week as a precaution, and several more were due for heavy pruning in May 2025. The article does not name this specific registered tree, so it neither confirms nor denies its survival; it is included because a reader walking this street should know the avenue is under active disease management and some of its chestnuts are coming down. The municipality is replanting one healthy tree for each one lost. Worth a recheck on the ground: ask whether the registered tree is still standing given the disease pressure on this street.
story:
In April 2025 the chestnut outside Spanjaardslaan 134 was taken down as a precaution, and several more along the street were listed for heavy pruning the month after. Bleeding canker has got into this avenue. A good share of its white and red horse chestnuts are in poor condition, and the council is putting back one healthy tree for every one it loses.

So this entry comes with a warning rather than a promise. The news report names the street, not the tree, and the national register records this one condition as unknown. It dates the planting to between 1900 and 1910, which makes the tree something like 120 years old and puts it on this street since before the cars were. Whether it is still standing is a question for whoever gets there next, and we would like to hear the answer.

Go in May and the point of the whole street is obvious anyway. Horse chestnuts flower in upright candles, white on the common kind and pink-red on the hybrids, and an avenue of them in flower is a better argument for street trees than any council report. This one is a white. For two weeks it is the reason anybody planted chestnuts along a road in the first place. The rest of the year it is a tree the neighbourhood is trying to keep.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in May by its flowers, white candles where several chestnuts along this avenue are the red-flowered kind. It stands in the line of chestnuts on the Spanjaardslaan itself, about 1.2 km north of the station.

best_time.label: May, when the avenue lights up in candles, white on this tree and red on its neighbours

name: The Turkey Oak of Rengerspark
age_estimate: roughly 116 to 126 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1695803, 'Moseik Rengerspark')
https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moseik (species identification: Dutch 'moseik' is the standard common name for Quercus cerris, Turkey oak)
access: Free. Open public park (Rengerspark, rijksmonument since 2001).
transport: About 1.2 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
verify_notes: Register nr 1695803. The register recorded the species field as null/unmapped ('species_unmapped: Moseik Rengerspark'); 'moseik' is Dutch for Quercus cerris, Turkey oak (confirmed via nl.wikipedia's Moseik article and multiple Dutch nursery/arboriculture sites), so this resolves cleanly rather than needing a reader question. Planted in the period the park was laid out (Rengerspark opened 1906, designed by Hendrik Copijn for the Rengers family gift of 1902), so a founding-era tree like the already-published maple (lee_014) and wingnut. The register calls it a healthy, fast-growing tree with an unusually stable structure and says it 'behoort tot een van de zwaarste moseiken van Nederland' (is among the heaviest Turkey oaks in the Netherlands), a superlative worth repeating per hard rule 8 since it comes straight from the register. No girth figure given despite the superlative claim; flag as not documented. Single-sourced beyond the species ID; no dedicated write-up of this specific tree found this pass.
story:
The national register calls this one of the heaviest Turkey oaks in the Netherlands, and then declines to say how thick it is. No girth, no height. Just the claim, and a note that the tree is healthy, fast growing and unusually stable in its structure.

The Dutch name for the species is moseik, moss oak, and it comes from the acorns. Every cup is covered in long whiskery scales that make it look mossed over, which is the one thing that separates a Turkey oak from the ordinary oaks of a Dutch park at ten paces. The register lists this tree under that name and nothing else, leaving the species column empty: Moseik Rengerspark.

The dates line up with the park around it. The Rengers family gave the ground to the city in 1902, Hendrik Copijn laid it out, and it opened in 1906. The register puts the oak planting between 1900 and 1910, so it has been here for as long as anyone has been allowed to walk through. The park itself has been a national monument since 2001, which is a rare thing for a piece of landscaping and tells you the design was worth protecting.

One person with a tape measure could settle the heaviest claim in a minute. Nobody has yet. If you do it, send us the number.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the acorn cups, whiskered all over with long mossy scales that no other oak in this park carries. It stands on the south side of Rengerspark.

best_time.label: September and October, when the mossy whiskered acorn cups come down

name: The Feather Elm of Vosseparkje (north-west)
species: Dutch Elm 'Exoniensis' (Ulmus x hollandica, feather elm cultivar)
age_estimate: roughly 116 to 126 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1692406, 'Pluimiep Vosseparkje')
access: Free. Open public park (Westerpark/Vosseparkje), open daily. Joins lee_016, lee_017 and lee_024 as the fourth registered tree in this small park.
transport: Short walk from Leeuwarden centre; the park sits just west of the Prinsentuin cluster.
verify_notes: Register nr 1692406, on the north side of the park (not the same specimen as lee_008's two Molenstraat feather elms, which stand on a street about 400m away). The park itself dates to 1872 (Gerrit Vlaskamp's drinking-water reservoir landscaping) and was redesigned in 1926. The register's own note is brief: 'een mooie pluimiep aan de noordzijde van het park' (a fine feather elm on the north side). A prior verification pass on 2026-09-09 fetched both the HCL 'Voetstappen in de Vosseparkwijk' walking-tour PDF and the HCL 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen' brochure (Westerpark stop, entry 16) and confirmed neither names a pluimiep in this park by description, and a direct WebSearch found nothing beyond the register. Single-sourced; delivered flagged rather than held, per the rule that an honest single-sourced tree beats silence. There is a second, separate feather elm in the same park (register nr 1692405, on the south-east side, see lee_032): treat as two distinct specimens of the same cultivar, not a duplicate.
story:
The park this elm stands in was laid out around the city's drinking water. In 1872 Gerrit Vlaskamp landscaped the grounds of a water reservoir on the west side of Leeuwarden, and the Vosseparkje is what became of it. The reservoir came first and the park followed. It was redesigned in 1926, by which point the elm was long in place: the register dates its planting to between 1900 and 1910.

Old elms are not a common sight in this country. Disease took most of them over the last century, which is reason enough to walk over to one that is 120 years old and still standing. This is a feather elm, pluimiep in Dutch, a cultivar that takes its name in both languages from the shape of the crown, upright and narrow where a common elm spreads wide.

The register's description of it runs to nine words: a fine feather elm on the north side of the park. That is the whole written record. The historical centre's walking tour of the Vosseparkwijk passes the park without naming it, and so does the city's monumental green route. Whatever else is known about this tree sits in somebody's memory rather than in an archive, and we would like to hear it.

A second feather elm of the same cultivar stands at the far end of the park, by the pond.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, a narrow upright plume where a common elm spreads into a vase. It stands on the north-west side of the Vosseparkje; its twin of the same cultivar is at the far end, by the pond.

name: The Feather Elm of Vosseparkje (south-east, by the pond)
species: Dutch Elm 'Exoniensis' (Ulmus x hollandica, feather elm cultivar)
age_estimate: roughly 116 to 126 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910

location.address: Westerpark / Vosseparkje, south-east side by the pond, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1692405, 'Pluimiep Vosseparkje')
access: Free. Open public park (Westerpark/Vosseparkje), open daily.
transport: Short walk from Leeuwarden centre; the park sits just west of the Prinsentuin cluster.
verify_notes: Register nr 1692405, on the south-east side of the park by the pond, roughly 250m from the north-west feather elm (nr 1692406, lee_031) of the same cultivar in the same small park. The register's own note: 'een fraaie standplaats heeft bij de vijver' (a fine spot by the pond). Same park history as the rest of the Vosseparkje cluster (1872 Vlaskamp landscaping around a drinking-water reservoir, redesigned 1926). No independent second source found this pass or the prior 2026-09-09 pass, which checked the same two HCL PDFs and WebSearch directly. Single-sourced, delivered flagged. Recognition note for the writer: the park now holds two feather elms of the same cultivar; anchor this one on the pond, since that is the one feature the register itself uses to place it, and say plainly that its twin stands elsewhere in the same park so a reader does not confuse the two.
story:
The national register says nothing about how big this elm is and rather a lot about where it stands: it has a fine spot by the pond. That is the entry, more or less in full. State inventories do not usually pay compliments to a view.

The Vosseparkje is small, a few minutes end to end, and seven of the trees in it are on that register. A Caucasian wingnut, a grey poplar, a leaning black locust, a Canadian poplar, an oak nobody has pinned to a species, and two feather elms of the same cultivar. This is the one by the water. Its counterpart stands about 250 metres off at the north-west end, which makes the pond the thing that tells them apart.

The ground was landscaped in 1872 by Gerrit Vlaskamp, around a reservoir built to hold the city's drinking water, and redrawn in 1926. The register dates this elm to between 1900 and 1910, so it was already standing when the 1926 plan was drawn and it is older than the park's present shape.

Nobody has written it up beyond the register. Two walking routes cover this neighbourhood, one from the city's historical centre and one following its monumental trees, and neither of them names the elm at the pond.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the water: it is the feather elm at the pond, its crown a narrow upright plume rather than a spreading vase. The park's other feather elm stands about 250 metres away at the north-west end.

name: The Canadian Poplar of Vosseparkje
age_estimate: roughly 126 to 136 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1692404, 'Canadese populier Vosseparkje')
access: Free. Open public park (Westerpark/Vosseparkje), open daily.
transport: Short walk from Leeuwarden centre; the park sits just west of the Prinsentuin cluster.
verify_notes: Register nr 1692404, west side of the park; not the same tree as the already-published Marilandica poplar (lee_007, register nr 1688390), which is a named cultivar in the Prinsentuin, a different park entirely. This is the plain Canadian poplar hybrid, planted a generation before the park's 1926 redesign. The register notes a heavy crown was advised for thinning in 2007, and that a 2016 check found the tree still standing, with some trunk-base damage from asphalt work near the base. No independent second source found this pass or the prior 2026-09-09 pass, which checked both HCL park PDFs and found the brochure's Prinsentuin stop describes a different Canadian poplar (the Marilandica). Single-sourced, delivered flagged. The register's own last-observed note (2016) is the most recent evidence of life; worth a recheck given ten years have passed.
story:
Canadian poplars are planted because they grow fast, and most of them are taken down long before they get to the age of this one. The register dates this tree to between 1890 and 1900, which makes it about 130 years old: a hybrid poplar that outlived the reason it was chosen.

It has been on the west side of the Vosseparkje since a generation before the park took its present shape in the 1926 redesign, and the paperwork on it reads like a medical file. In 2007 its crown had grown heavy enough that thinning was advised. A check in 2016 found it standing, with damage at the foot of the trunk where asphalt work had come too close. That 2016 note is the most recent word anybody has written about it, and it is ten years old, so if you walk past we would like to hear that the tree is still there.

Leeuwarden has one other Canadian poplar on the national register, a named cultivar in the Prinsentuin on the far side of the centre. That one gets the walking routes and the brochures. This one, the plain hybrid at the edge of a small park, gets a line in a register and a note about the asphalt.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, triangular and green on both faces, where the park's grey poplar is white-felted underneath. It stands on the west side of the Vosseparkje, scarred at the foot where asphalt work came close.

name: The Oak at the South-East Entrance of Vosseparkje
species: Oak, species not established (Quercus sp., possibly Caucasian or Persian oak per the register's own name)
age_estimate: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1686956, 'Kaukasische/Perzische eik')
access: Free. Open public park (Westerpark/Vosseparkje), open daily; stands right at the south-east entrance.
transport: Short walk from Leeuwarden centre; the park sits just west of the Prinsentuin cluster.
verify_notes: Register nr 1686956, at the south-east entrance to the park, one of the oldest plantings in this cluster (1870-1880, a decade or more before most of the park's other registered trees). The register's own name is ambiguous between two species, 'Kaukasische/Perzische eik' (Caucasian oak, Quercus macranthera, or Persian oak, Quercus castaneifolia), and gives no further detail ('site_history: onbekend'); recorded here as species not established rather than guessed, per the publish-and-ask rule. Not the same tree as the other register oak at the former Schapenweide/Aegon office site (nr 1682942, blocked as private land, see leads file): different coordinate, over 500m away, on public park ground rather than a corporate campus. No independent second source found this pass. Single-sourced, delivered flagged.
story:
The national register cannot decide what this tree is. Its entry reads Caucasian/Persian oak, with a slash doing the work that a species name usually does, and there is nothing else in the file: the site history field says unknown.

Both candidates behind that slash are eastern trees standing a long way outside their range. Quercus macranthera comes from the Caucasus and carries big lobed leaves with felt on the underside. Quercus castaneifolia comes from the same mountains and from northern Iran, and its leaves look like a sweet chestnut's, long and edged with sharp teeth. Whichever of the two this is, it is not one of the oaks native to the Netherlands.

It is the oldest of the seven registered trees in this park. The planting band, 1870 to 1880, overlaps the years Gerrit Vlaskamp was landscaping the reservoir grounds that became the Vosseparkje in 1872, though nothing on record says the oak went in with that work. It has held the south-east entrance ever since, which means most people who use this park walk straight past it on their way to look at something else.

We would rather ask than guess. If you can read an oak leaf, go and settle which of the two it is, and tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the oak at the gate rather than one of the Dutch natives, its leaves either chestnut-toothed or big and felted underneath. It stands right at the south-east entrance of the Vosseparkje.

name: The Pollard Limes of the Liauckama House
age_estimate: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840

location.address: Grote Kerkstraat 9, in front of the Liauckama House (part of Museum Princessehof), Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1682919, two pollarded limes, planted band 1830-1840)
access: Free. Stand on the public street (Grote Kerkstraat) in front of the building, register setting weg (road).
transport: Central Leeuwarden, short walk from Leeuwarden Centraal station, in the museum quarter around the Prinsentuin.
story:
One of these two limes carries a cavity in its trunk the shape of a letterbox.

They stand as a matched pair in front of the Liauckama House on the Grote Kerkstraat, and both are pollards: trees cut back to the same points, over and over. A tree answers that treatment by thickening the cut ends into knuckles and throwing a burst of young shoots off the top of them, so a pollard lime ends up short, heavy and knobbled where a free-grown lime would be tall and even. The knuckles are the tally of every cut.

The building behind them is much older. The Liauckama House goes back to the second half of the sixteenth century, possibly 1580, and is now part of Museum Princessehof. The trees came far later, and the national register cannot quite decide when. Its planting band puts them at 1830 to 1840, while its own history text for this pair says they have probably stood on this spot for over two hundred years. The two readings sit a good half-century apart, and both of them are the register's.

The register calls this a striking place for a tree to stand, and rates both of them fair to reasonable in condition. Nobody else has written them up, so if you know more, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the pollard knuckles, two short heavy trunks each topped with a fist of cut ends and a burst of young shoots. They stand as a pair on the Grote Kerkstraat; the eastern one has a letterbox-shaped cavity.

name: The Adoption Beech of the Sint Anthony Gasthuis
age_estimate: roughly 156 to 166 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870

location.address: Voortuin (front garden) of the Nieuw Sint Anthony Gasthuis, Perkswaltje, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1682926, planted band 1860-1870, visitable=ja, owner=publiekrechtelijke organisatie)

OpenStreetMap (queried 2026-09-10): the Nieuw Sint Anthonygasthuis building (wikidata Q15879818, rce heritage id 24160) fronts onto Perkswaltje, tagged access=private/foot=permissive, i.e. a courtyard walkway pedestrians may use even though it is not a through public road
access: Free to view from the almshouse's front garden/courtyard. The street it fronts, Perkswaltje, is a permissive pedestrian route rather than a fully public road (OSM tags it access=private, foot=permissive), consistent with the register's own visitable=ja. Not the same site as the Sint Anthony Gasthuis entries at Perkswaltje 11 already excluded from this project as private (a different part of the same almshouse complex, owner=stichting there vs owner=publiekrechtelijke organisatie here).
transport: Central Leeuwarden, short walk from Leeuwarden Centraal station.
story:
This copper beech used to have a twin. Look at the other side of the front garden and you will find a ginkgo.

The Nieuw Sint Anthony Gasthuis was built between 1862 and 1864 to a design by F. Stoett, and two copper beeches went into its front garden, one on each side, each mirroring the other. The national register puts their planting somewhere between 1860 and 1870 and suspects, without stating it as fact, that they arrived with the building itself. That would make this one around 160 years old.

The western tree lost. A wound opened in its trunk, a fungus nobody identified got into it, and it declined quickly. When inspectors came back in 2017 they found it had been felled and a ginkgo planted where it had stood. Symmetry is a hard thing to hold on to for a century and a half.

The eastern tree is the one still standing, and it has been looked after. The Bomenstichting made it their adoption tree in 1987, and the register still describes it as in good condition. Look down at the base of the trunk: the boundary fence has been cut and reshaped around the tree rather than the other way round.

The register carries no measurement of the trunk, and only one coordinate for what were once two trees, so the pin marks the garden rather than the beech.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the purple-black leaves, and by what stands opposite it: a ginkgo, planted where its twin was felled. It stands on the eastern side of the front garden of the Nieuw Sint Anthony Gasthuis.

name: The Twin Beeches of the Goverts Gasthuis
age_estimate: roughly 116 to 126 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1682928, two beeches planted in symmetric layout, planted band 1900-1910)

https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcelis_Goverts_Gasthuis (building history: founded 1658, this Noordersingel almshouse built 1877 to a design by H.R. Stoett; corroborates the register's own building-history note, not the trees themselves)
access: Free to view. The almshouse's garden faces the public Noordersingel street, directly across from the Prinsentuin; register marks the trees visitable=ja, owned by the almshouse's public-body trust.
transport: Central Leeuwarden, short walk from the Prinsentuin cluster.
story:
These two beeches were dated by a photograph. In a picture of the almshouse taken in 1904 they are saplings, thin enough to be easy to miss.

That photograph is most of the evidence for their age, and the national register says so plainly. It reads the picture, puts the planting somewhere between 1900 and 1910, and leaves the question there. It also notes what the image makes obvious: the two were set deliberately in mirror image, one on each side of the building, the way an institution used to announce itself.

The institution is far older than either the trees or the house they stand against. The Marcelis Goverts Gasthuis was founded in 1658 by Marcelis Goverts and Mayke Marcus for Leeuwarden's Mennonite congregation, and it moved to the Noordersingel in 1877 into a Neo-Renaissance building by the architect H.R. Stoett. The beeches came a generation after that.

The most dangerous thing to happen to them since went on underground. In 1994 sewer works were dug close by, the kind of job that quietly kills a mature tree by taking out its roots, and both came through it. Inspected in 2017, both were in good leaf with nothing wrong at the base of the trunk.

Neither trunk has been measured, and the register is the only source that mentions the trees at all. They stand directly across the Noordersingel from the Prinsentuin, which puts them on the same short walk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the symmetry: two beeches of matching size set one on each side of the almshouse front, planted to mirror the building. They stand on the Noordersingel, across from the Prinsentuin.

name: The Second Plane of the Old City Cemetery
age_estimate: roughly 166 to 176 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860

location.address: Oude Stadsbegraafplaats, Jelsummerstraat, on the path between sections 2 and 4

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1692402, planted band 1850-1860)

https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oude_Stadsbegraafplaats_Leeuwarden (independently confirms the cemetery's 1830 design by Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, 1833 opening and 1967 national-monument status, matching the register's own account of the site; does not mention this specific tree)
access: Free. Open ground, a former cemetery no longer in use, the same site as the already-published plane (lee_004) on the path between sections 2 and 3.
transport: About 1.5 km north of Leeuwarden station, on the Jelsummerstraat.
story:
The register gives this cemetery two separate plane entries, and they stand half a kilometre apart inside the same walled ground.

This is the second of them: a pair of planes on the path between sections two and four, with a planting band of 1850 to 1860. The oldest trees here date from around 1830, so these two arrived a good twenty years into the cemetery's working life, when the ground they shade had already been filling for a generation.

That ground was laid out in 1833 to a design by Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, who also drew the Prinsentuin, which is why a burial ground reads here as a landscape garden with graves in it. Burials stopped long ago and the site became a national monument in 1967.

What it has become since is closer to a wood. Ivy has climbed most of the trunks. Grey herons nest in the crowns, colonially and noisily, and they start early enough in the year that the racket arrives before the leaves do.

The planes themselves do what planes do everywhere. The bark comes away in plates and leaves a mottle of cream, olive and grey underneath, which makes them the easiest trunks to pick out among all the ivy around them.

Neither of the two has been measured, and the register is the only source that records them. If you know more about this pair than a planting decade, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the flaking cream and olive bark, and by there being two side by side. They stand on the path between sections 2 and 4; the cemetery's other registered plane is a single tree 500 metres off.

name: The Silver Lime of Sophiaplantsoen
age_estimate: roughly 116 to 126 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1682940, planted band 1900-1910, owner=gemeente, visitable=ja)
access: Free, on the public Sophiaplantsoen green strip near Lange Marktstraat and the station area. Checked against OpenStreetMap (2026-09-10): the surrounding streets (Sophialaan, Van Swietenstraat, Lange Marktstraat) are ordinary public roads and cycleways with no access=private tags, unlike the nearby former Schapenweide estate ground now occupied by the Aegon office campus about 100m away, which this project has already excluded as private (see data/leads/leeuwarden.json). This is a different, public corner of the old Schapenweide name.
transport: Near Leeuwarden station, on the Sophiaplantsoen/Lange Marktstraat side.
story:
The national register carries these two limes, and in the space where it keeps a tree's history it has written one word: onbekend. Unknown.

What it does record is short. Two silver limes on the Sophiaplantsoen, planted somewhere between 1900 and 1910, owned by the city, free for anyone walking past. That is the whole file on them.

The species is the interesting part. Tilia tomentosa comes from the Balkans and Anatolia rather than from anywhere near Friesland, and the give-away sits on the back of the leaf: dense white felt underneath, dark green on the face. Turn one leaf over and you have the species.

Leeuwarden turns out to hold a small collection of them. One stands on the Druifstreek opposite the Blokhuispoort, another north of it on the Eewal, and this pair a few minutes from the station, which is enough to make silver lime a species you can tick off across a single afternoon in one city.

Nobody has taped either trunk, and nothing has been written about the pair beyond the register's two lines. If you know when they went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by there being two of the same tree side by side, and by the leaf undersides, felted white where the common limes around town are green on both faces. They stand on the Sophiaplantsoen strip.

name: The Beech of Diaconessenpark
age_estimate: roughly 136 to 146 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: Diaconessenpark, in front of the former main building of the Diakonessenziekenhuis, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1688395, planted band 1880-1890)
access: Free. About 75m from the already-published Diaconessenpark trees (lee_019, lee_020, lee_021), the same landscaped courtyard of the 1990s apartment redevelopment of the former Diakonessenhuis hospital grounds. An earlier pass established via OSM that this whole courtyard is mapped leisure=park with open, gate-free, paved footways and no private-access tags; that finding is extended here since this tree sits inside the same courtyard.
transport: About 700 m from Leeuwarden Centraal station, in the Diaconessenpark courtyard.
story:
The flats around this beech went up in the 1990s. The tree was already a century old when the builders arrived.

What stood here before them was the Diakonessenhuis, Leeuwarden's deaconess hospital, which closed in 1987 and had its grounds turned into apartments over the decade that followed. The old garden came through the conversion as a courtyard, paved through and open at every side, and it still holds its trees. Three more of them are mapped about 75 metres from this one.

This is the least documented of the set. The national register gives it a planting band of 1880 to 1890 and then stops. The history field is empty. The red chestnut down the courtyard has a written record behind it, of the hospital garden it was planted for and of the root damage the 1990s building work did to it; the beech has nothing attached at all, so what it went through during that decade of digging is simply not on record.

You can still pick it out. Common beech carries bark like nothing else of its size: smooth, pale grey and close to unbroken, more skin than bark, where the chestnuts around it are rough and plated.

The register lists it as privately owned, as it does two of the three trees already mapped in this courtyard, which is a fact about the deeds rather than about a gate.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bark, smooth pale grey and close to unbroken, where the chestnuts sharing the courtyard are rough and plated. It stands in the Diaconessenpark courtyard, in front of the former hospital's main building.

name: The Caucasian Wingnut of Rengerspark
age_estimate: roughly 116 to 126 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (LRMB register nr 1695807, planted with the park's founding, 1900-1910)

https://web.archive.org/web/20250522131935/https://www.welkominleeuwarden.nl/stem-op-de-mooiste-boom-van-de-gemeente-leeuwarden/ (2020 municipal 'Most Beautiful Tree' public vote: 'de grote vleugelnoot in het Rengerspark' was one of ten trees nominated, confirming the tree's local recognition and standing as of 2020)
access: Free. Open public park (Rengerspark, rijksmonument since 2001).
transport: About 1.2 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot; joins the already-published maple (lee_014) and Turkey oak (lee_030) in the same park.
story:
A large branch tore out of this tree and took much of the trunk with it. What is left stands as two halves, held by an anchor braced between them.

The national register is not alarmed by that. It calls this wingnut one of the heaviest of its species in the Netherlands and the undisputed champion of Friesland, reads the wound as an early entry into the veteran phase, and says the tree can safely carry on for at least another decade. It is being left to age and decay where it stands, deliberately, for the wildlife that a rotting tree of this size supports.

Rengerspark was a gift. The Rengers family handed the ground to Leeuwarden, Hendrik Copijn laid it out between 1902 and 1906, and the wingnut went in with that planting. In 2020 the municipality ran a public vote for the most beautiful tree in the district, and the big wingnut in Rengerspark was one of the ten on the ballot.

Late summer is its moment. Caucasian wingnut is a walnut relative from the Caucasus, and it fruits in long green strings of winged nutlets that hang off the branches like beads on a curtain.

For a champion it is strangely unmeasured: no girth, no height, no figure of any kind on record anywhere we can find. If you own a tape measure, we would like the number.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, split into two halves by a torn-out branch and held by an anchor braced between them. It stands on the south side of Rengerspark; no other tree here hangs strings of winged nutlets in late summer.

best_time.label: August and September, when the long strings of winged nutlets hang from the branches
